headline: A Secret Test Reveals That AI Companies Aren't Always Keeping Your Data Private

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: A computer expert wanted to find out if information people type into AI chatbots stays private. So he made a clever test. He created fake secret codes, like pretend passwords, that nobody had ever used before. He typed each fake secret into a message sent to an AI company. Since the secrets were fake, he could watch exactly what happened to them. Many AI apps don't go straight to one company. Instead, messages pass through several different companies, like a relay race, before reaching the AI. The test showed a big problem. Some companies got broken into by hackers, who stole the secrets and tried to use them. Other companies secretly kept copies of messages even when they promised not to look at them. Some even peeked at private web links hidden inside the messages, days after they were sent. This matters because many people share private details with AI chatbots, thinking it is safe. This test shows that isn't always true. Experts say the safest choice is to use AI companies you trust directly, instead of ones that pass your words through many middlemen.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: A security researcher named HD Moore ran an experiment to see whether private information shared with AI chatbots actually stays private. He created about two million fake secrets, things like password keys and website links that had never existed before, and slipped one into each message sent to AI services. Because the secrets were brand new and completely under his control, he could tell exactly who looked at them or tried to use them. Many popular AI apps don't talk to just one AI company. Instead, they use 'routers' that forward your message to whichever company can answer it cheapest or fastest, sometimes passing through several different companies along the way. Each stop can read your message before sending it along. The results were alarming. Hackers had broken into at least three AI providers and were stealing the secret information the moment it arrived. Some companies that resell AI services were secretly saving and misusing messages to earn more money. Even companies that promised 'we won't save your data' were caught doing exactly that, including one company that quietly visited private web links hidden inside messages. This matters because millions of people trust AI tools with personal or sensitive information every day. The experiment proves that promises of privacy aren't always kept, and that your words may pass through more hands than you realize.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: To test whether AI companies truly protect the private information people type into chatbots, researcher HD Moore designed a clever trap. He created nearly two million fake 'secrets,' such as unused passwords and private web addresses, and hid one inside each message sent to different AI services. Since each secret was brand new and controlled only by him, any time it got used or visited later, he knew exactly which company was responsible. This revealed how complicated the AI system really is. Many apps don't talk directly to one AI company. Instead, they use go-between services, sometimes called AI routers or gateways, that forward each message to whichever AI model can handle it for the lowest price. A single message might pass through two or three companies before getting a reply, and each one can read the plain, unscrambled text along the way. The findings were troubling. At least three AI hosting companies had been secretly hacked, and the attackers stole incoming messages the instant they arrived, even ones marked as private with 'Zero Data Retention,' a setting meant to guarantee nothing gets saved. Other companies that resell AI access were found quietly logging and reusing people's messages to make extra money, something Moore proved by sending the same request through different sellers and comparing results. Perhaps most striking, one AI company based in China was caught secretly visiting private web links hidden in prompts sent to it, even requests from U.S. companies that claimed their customers' data stayed inside the U.S. This matters because people increasingly use AI tools for everything from schoolwork to business plans, often assuming their words disappear after they hit send. This research shows that assumption can be false, and that the paths information travels through online are far messier and less secure than most users realize.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: Security researcher HD Moore ran a large-scale experiment to test a question many people assume is already answered: does information typed into AI chatbots actually stay private? To find out, he planted nearly two million unique, trackable 'secrets,' fake AWS cloud access keys, unused passwords, and private web links, into prompts sent to a wide range of AI services. Because each secret was new and entirely under his control, any later use of it could be traced back to the exact company responsible, much like how a canary once warned coal miners of danger before they could sense it themselves. Modern AI apps rarely connect to a single company. Instead, they often rely on 'AI routers' or 'gateways,' middleman services that forward a user's prompt to whichever underlying AI model can answer it most cheaply or efficiently. A message can bounce through multiple companies before producing a reply, and at every stop, it exists as readable, unscrambled text that can be logged, copied, or misused. The results exposed serious failures across this hidden supply chain. At least three AI hosting providers had been breached by hackers who intercepted incoming prompts the moment they arrived, sometimes within hours, then used stolen access keys to explore cloud storage systems, attempt to activate paid AI models, and create secret backup accounts for themselves, racking up tens of thousands of unauthorized actions. Alarmingly, some of the stolen prompts were labeled with privacy protections like 'Zero Data Retention,' a setting meant to guarantee no storage of user data, proving that privacy settings are meaningless once an attacker has already broken in. Separately, some AI resellers that offered suspiciously cheap prices were caught quietly logging customer prompts themselves, apparently to profit from the data. Perhaps the most striking discovery involved a major Chinese AI lab, whose systems were caught secretly retrieving private web links embedded in more than half of all prompts sent to it, including two-thirds of those marked private, even when customers had gone through U.S.-based resale companies specifically to keep their data inside the United States. This research matters because AI tools are now deeply embedded in schools, businesses, and everyday life, and users routinely trust them with sensitive details. The experiment demonstrates that this trust is frequently misplaced, and that meaningful privacy currently requires choosing providers carefully, understanding how data travels, or accepting that convenience often comes at the cost of security.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: In an ambitious effort to test whether privacy promises made by the AI industry hold up in practice, security researcher HD Moore, chief research officer at the firm Dragos, designed an ingenious large-scale experiment. He generated nearly two million unique, previously unused 'secrets,' including AWS cloud access keys, SSH passwords, private web URLs, and git repository references, and embedded exactly one into each prompt sent across a wide variety of AI services. Because every secret was fabricated and entirely under his control, any later access to it could be traced precisely to whichever party was responsible, functioning much like the canaries once carried into coal mines to detect danger invisible to humans. This method exposed the hidden architecture behind many popular AI applications. Rather than connecting directly to a single company, these apps frequently rely on intermediary services called AI routers or gateways, such as OpenRouter or Vercel, which examine incoming prompts in order to forward them to whichever underlying AI model offers the best combination of price and capability. A single prompt may pass through several companies, sometimes bouncing between multiple routers, with each link in the chain decrypting and reading the plaintext content before passing it along, typically logging it according to its own retention policy, if any. The experiment's findings were damning across multiple categories. At least three AI hosting providers had been actively compromised by hackers, who intercepted incoming prompts, including ones flagged under 'Zero Data Retention' policies, within hours of their arrival. These attackers then used the stolen AWS credentials to probe cloud storage buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores for additional access, attempted to activate paid AI models through AWS Bedrock, and created unauthorized administrative accounts to maintain long-term access, ultimately generating tens of thousands of fraudulent API calls. Evidence even suggested a single adversary was behind breaches at two separate providers, since stolen credentials from both surfaced almost simultaneously from the same rented server. Separately, some AI resellers were found to be deliberately undercutting competitors on price specifically to attract traffic, then quietly logging and exploiting the prompts they received, a practice Moore confirmed by routing identical requests through different sellers and comparing outcomes. Most strikingly, a major Chinese AI lab was caught retrieving secret URLs embedded in more than half of all prompts sent to its models, including roughly two-thirds of requests explicitly marked as private or 'no data collection,' and this behavior persisted even when American companies resold the lab's models under the impression that customer data would remain within the United States. Moore's ultimate recommendation is sobering: the only fully reliable protection is hosting AI models on private, self-owned servers, an option few individuals or small organizations can afford. Short of that, he advises choosing a single, reputable first-tier provider directly, rather than routing through resale marketplaces, since fewer intermediaries mean fewer opportunities for data to be intercepted, logged, or misused. The research underscores a broader truth about the current AI ecosystem: contractual privacy promises offer little protection once systems are compromised or when business incentives favor quietly harvesting user data.

questions: If you found out a homework help app or chatbot you use was secretly saving your questions, how would that change the way you use it?
Why do you think companies promise 'privacy' or 'no data collection' even when they might not be able to fully guarantee it, and what responsibility should they have when that promise is broken?

Since many apps and websites pass your information through multiple companies you never see, what steps could schools, families, or lawmakers take to better protect people's private information online?
